solution.en:
Use vile, vial.

Vile [नीच, दुष्ट] is an adjective describing the sorcerer: wicked or evil.
Vial [शीशी] is a noun: a small glass container, here holding poison.

Complete sentence: The vile sorcerer upturned the vial of poison into the goblet, his lips curling into a smirk.

veil — a piece of cloth covering the face [घूँघट, परदा]
vail — an old word meaning to lower or take off (as a hat) [झुकाना (पुरातन)]

question.en: Which of the following options is NOT one of the meanings of the homonym 'compound'? [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: A substance formed from two or more elements chemically combined

2.en: A building or group of buildings enclosed by a barrier

3.en: To make something worse by adding to it

4.en: To subtract or reduce gradually over time

solution.en:
To subtract or reduce gradually over time is not a meaning of “compound”.

Compound can mean:
a chemical substance formed from two or more elements [यौगिक]
an enclosed area containing buildings [अहाता, परिसर]
to make a problem worse by adding to it [और बिगाड़ना]

It also means to combine, or to add interest to interest (compound interest) — the opposite of reducing.

question.en: Which of the following options is not one of the meanings of the homonym 'project'? [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: A planned piece of work to achieve a goal

2.en: To extend outward or stick out

3.en: A protective structure used in military defence

solution.en:
A protective structure used in military defence is not a meaning of “project”.

Project can mean:
a planned piece of work [परियोजना]
to stick out or extend outward [बाहर निकला होना]
to estimate or forecast [अनुमान लगाना]

A protective defensive structure is a bastion or rampart, not a project.

question.en: Which sentence has the correct homonym? [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

2.en: They build a new capitel for the state.

4.en: They lived in the capital building.

solution.en:
Capital has several meanings; one is "punishable by death", as in capital punishment [मृत्युदंड]. Sentence 1 uses it correctly.
Sentence 2 misspells the word ("capitel"), sentence 3 should read "capital letter", and sentence 4 should use "Capitol" (a legislative building), in which people do not live.

Option meanings
Capital — (1) city where the government sits [राजधानी]; (2) large letter [बड़ा अक्षर]; (3) punishable by death [मृत्युदंड योग्य]; (4) wealth, money [पूँजी]
Capitol — a building where a legislature meets, e.g. the US Capitol [विधान भवन]

question.en: Which of the following options is NOT one of the meanings of the homonym 'current'? [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: The movement of a body of water or air

3.en: A small dried grape used in making buns and cakes

4.en: Happening or existing at the present time

solution.en:
Current (adjective) means happening at present; as a noun it means a flow of water or air, or a flow of electricity.
"A small dried grape used in buns and cakes" is a currant [छोटी सूखी किशमिश], a different word with a different spelling (a homophone), not a meaning of "current".

Option meanings
The movement of a body of water or air — current [धारा]
Electricity flowing through a wire — electric current [विद्युत धारा]
A small dried grape — currant, not current [छोटी सूखी किशमिश]
Happening or existing at the present time — current [वर्तमान]

question.en: Which of the following options is NOT one of the meanings of the homonym 'contract'? [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

2.en: A written or spoken agreement enforceable by law

solution.en:
Contract can mean a legal agreement [अनुबंध], to shrink or become smaller [सिकुड़ना], or to catch a disease [रोग से ग्रस्त होना].
"To express disapproval or disappointment" is not a meaning of "contract"; that idea is expressed by words like deplore or frown on.

Option meanings
To express disapproval — not a meaning of contract [अस्वीकृति व्यक्त करना]
A written or spoken agreement enforceable by law — contract (noun) [अनुबंध]
To shrink or become smaller — contract (verb) [सिकुड़ना]
To catch or develop (a disease) — contract (verb) [रोग लगना]

question.en: Which of the following options is NOT one of the meanings of the homonym 'obscure'? [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: To make something unclear or difficult to understand

2.en: Not well-known or not easily seen

3.en: To hide or conceal something partially

4.en: To look at something from an alternative perspective

solution.en:
Obscure can mean not well known or not easily seen (adjective) [अज्ञात, अस्पष्ट], to make unclear or difficult to understand (verb) [अस्पष्ट करना], or to hide partially (verb) [ढक देना].
"To look at something from an alternative perspective" is not a meaning of "obscure".

Option meanings
To make something unclear — obscure (verb) [अस्पष्ट करना]
Not well-known or not easily seen — obscure (adjective) [गुमनाम, अस्पष्ट]
To hide or conceal partially — obscure (verb) [छिपाना]
To look at something from another perspective — not a meaning of obscure [दूसरे दृष्टिकोण से देखना]

question.en: Which of the following is NOT a meaning of the homonym 'recess'? [Steno 11 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

2.en: A break or pause in proceedings, especially in school or court

4.en: A hollow space or indentation in a wall

solution.en:
"Slow backward movement and disappearance" is the meaning of recession/receding, not of recess [अवकाश, आला].

Remote part — a secluded or inner part, e.g. the recesses of the mind [गहन भाग]
Hollow — an indentation or alcove in a wall [आला, ताख]

Related words: Recess: interval, niche, alcove.

question.en: Which of the following options is NOT one of the meanings of the homonym 'tender'? [Steno 11 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

question.en:

question.en:

Palate [तालु; रुचि/परख] — the sense of taste; figuratively, a person's taste or appreciation (here, for subtle tones).
Palette [रंग-पट्टिका] — the board on which an artist mixes colours (where the delicate hues are).

question.en: Pick the odd Homonym from the following. [Steno 12 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

solution.en:
Homophones (words sharing identical pronunciation but differing in spelling and meaning):
• Flee (/fliː/) — to run away from danger [भाग जाना]
• Flea (/fliː/) — a small wingless jumping insect [पिस्सू]
Both 'flee' and 'flea' are exact homophones sharing identical pronunciation. 'Flees' is simply the 3rd person singular of flee.
• Free (/friː/) has a completely distinct consonant sound (/fr/ instead of /fl/) and does not share phonetics with 'flee/flea'.
Therefore, Free is the odd word out.

question.en: Which of the following is NOT the meaning of the homonym 'resort'? [Steno 12 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

1.en: A place frequently visited for a specific purpose

2.en: A popular holiday or vacation destination

3.en: To arrange things again in a particular order

4.en: To adopt a strategy, especially as a last option

solution.en:
Examine the standard polysemous meanings of the noun/verb resort:
1. Noun: A popular vacation or holiday destination with amenities [विश्राम स्थल, सैरगाह] (Option 2).
2. Noun: A place frequently visited for recreation or a specific activity (Option 1).
3. Verb: To turn to and adopt a course of action, typically an undesirable or last-choice measure ('resort to violence') [सहारा लेना] (Option 4).
• The definition 'To arrange things again in a particular order' corresponds to re-sort (with a hyphen, meaning to sort again), which is NOT a meaning of the single word 'resort'.
Therefore, Option 3 is NOT a meaning of the homonym 'resort'.

question.en: Which of the following options is NOT one of the meanings of the homonym 'restraint'? [Steno 12 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

1.en: A measure or condition that keeps someone or something under control

3.en: A device used to limit movement

4.en: The ability to control one's own emotions or actions

solution.en:
Examine the standard semantic meanings of restraint:
1. The act of holding back, or self-control over impulses/emotions (e.g., 'show restraint') [आत्म-नियंत्रण] (Option 4).
2. A physical device that restricts movement (e.g., seatbelts, handcuffs) [बंधन, रोकने वाला उपकरण] (Option 3).
3. A rule, measure, or condition that regulates freedom of action (Option 1).
• 'An extremely stressful situation' refers to duress, distress, or strain, NOT 'restraint'.
Therefore, Option 2 is NOT one of the meanings of 'restraint'.

(Q) The legal process of officially forming and registering a new corporation or business entity [Selection Post (Graduate) 22 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

solution.en:
Meaning: The term Incorporation refers biologically/physically to combining or taking in something as part of a whole, and legally to the formation and registration of a corporate entity.
Assimilation applies only to biological or cultural absorption, not corporate registration.
Calcination and Acquisition do not satisfy both definitions.
Vocab Meanings:
• Incorporation: Including something as part of a whole; forming a legal company (समावेशन / निगमन - कंपनी का पंजीकरण)
• Assimilation: Absorbing and integrating something (आत्मसात्करण / समावेश)
• Calcination: Heating a substance to a high temperature (निस्तापन)
• Acquisition: Buying or obtaining something (अधिग्रहण)

solution.en:
Rule: Words that have the same pronunciation but differ in meaning, origin, and spelling are called homophones.
Both 'soul' (the spiritual aspect of a person) and 'sole' (the underside of a shoe) are pronounced identically (/soʊl/).
Homonyms usually share spelling or pronunciation, homographs share the exact spelling, and polysemy refers to a single word carrying multiple related meanings.

• Homonyms: Words with the same spelling or sound but different meanings (समनाम / समरूपी शब्द)
• Polysemy: One word having several related meanings (बहुअर्थकता)
• Homographs: Words spelt the same but differing in meaning or sound (समवर्तनी शब्द)

question.en:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
"The architect could have been designing the building." [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

2.en: The building could have been designed.

3.en: The building could be being designed.

4.en: The building could have been being designed.

solution.en:
Rule
Modal perfect continuous (could have been + V-ing) becomes could have been being + past participle in the passive.

Explicit changes
The object “the building” becomes the subject.
“could have been designing” becomes “could have been being designed”.
The agent “by the architect” may be dropped, as in the options.

Final sentence
The building could have been being designed.

Options 1 and 2 lose the continuous aspect, and option 3 loses the perfect aspect.

question.en:
Select the correct active form.
"Such mistakes are not expected to be made by trained professionals." [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

1.en: Trained professionals are not making such mistakes.

2.en: Trained professionals are not expected to make such mistakes.

3.en: Trained professionals should not have made such mistakes.

solution.en:
Rule
In “are not expected to be made by…”, only the infinitive is passive; make the infinitive active and keep “are not expected”.

Explicit changes
The agent “trained professionals” becomes the subject.
“to be made” becomes “to make”.
“Such mistakes” becomes the object of “make”.

Final sentence
Trained professionals are not expected to make such mistakes.

The other options change the meaning (a present action, a past criticism or a habit) instead of converting the voice.

question.en:
Identify the correct active voice transformation of the following sentence:
"Her routine work has been completed by my mother." [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

1.en: My mother has been completing her routine work.

2.en: My mother has completed routine work

3.en: My mother has completed her routine work

4.en: My mother has been completed her routine work

solution.en:
Rule
Present perfect passive (has been + V3) becomes present perfect active (has + V3).

Explicit changes
The agent “my mother” becomes the subject.
“has been completed” becomes “has completed”.
“Her routine work” becomes the object.

Final sentence
My mother has completed her routine work.

Option 1 uses “has completing”, option 2 drops “her” and the capital letter, and option 4 wrongly keeps “been”.

question.en:
Change the following sentence into the Active form.
His application had been looked over by a special committee for weeks. [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

1.en: A special committee has looked over his application for weeks.

2.en: A special committee was looking over his application for weeks.

3.en: A special committee had been looking over his application for weeks.

4.en: His application was looked over by a special committee.

solution.en:
Rule
Past perfect passive (had been + V3) corresponds to the past perfect in the active; with “for weeks”, the action is a continuing one up to a past point.

Explicit changes
The agent “a special committee” becomes the subject.
“His application” becomes the object of “looking over”.
The past perfect time frame is kept with “had”; “for weeks” shows duration, which the continuous form expresses.

Final sentence
A special committee had been looking over his application for weeks.

The strict form “had looked over” is not offered; options 1 and 2 change the time frame and option 4 is still passive.

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.
Take a pair of binoculars with you lest you all should miss the chance of looking at the distant scenes. [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: Let a pair of binoculars be taken with you lest the chance of looking at the distant scenes would missed by you all.

2.en: Let a pair of binoculars taken with you lest the chance of looking at the distant scenes should be missed by you all.

3.en: Let a pair of binoculars be taken with you otherwise the chance of looking at the distant scenes would be missed by you all.

4.en: Let a pair of binoculars be taken with you lest the chance of looking at the distant scenes should be missed by you all.

solution.en:
Rule
An imperative becomes Let + object + be + past participle; the “lest … should” clause also turns passive: lest + new subject + should be + past participle.

Explicit changes
“Take a pair of binoculars with you” → “Let a pair of binoculars be taken with you”.
“you all should miss the chance” → “the chance … should be missed by you all”.
Keep “lest”; it is followed by “should”.

Final sentence
Let a pair of binoculars be taken with you lest the chance of looking at the distant scenes should be missed by you all.

Option 1 has “would missed”, option 2 omits “be”, and option 3 replaces “lest … should” with “otherwise … would”.

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.
The tiger ate all the flesh that the zoo-keeper had kept in the enclosure. [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: All the flesh that had been kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure was eaten by the tiger.

2.en: All the flesh that was kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure was eaten by the tiger.

3.en: All the flesh that had been kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure had been eaten by the tiger.

4.en: All the flesh that was kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure had been eaten by the tiger.

solution.en:
Rule
Change both clauses: simple past (ate) → was/were + V3; past perfect (had kept) → had been + V3.

Explicit changes
“all the flesh” becomes the subject of the main clause: “was eaten by the tiger”.
The relative clause becomes “that had been kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure”.

Final sentence
All the flesh that had been kept by the zoo-keeper in the enclosure was eaten by the tiger.

Option 2 changes the past perfect, and options 3 and 4 change the simple past of the main clause.

From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

1.en: It was exclaimed by Suruchi that a very big dorsal fin was possessed by the fish.

2.en: It was exclaimed by Suruchi that a very big dorsal fin had been possessed by the fish.

3.en: Suruchi exclaimed that a very big dorsal fin is possessed by the fish.

4.en: It exclaimed Suruchi that a very big dorsal fin was possessed by the fish.

solution.en:
Rule
Both clauses are in the simple past. The main clause becomes “It was exclaimed by Suruchi that…”, and the that-clause becomes “was + past participle”.

Explicit changes
“Suruchi exclaimed” → “It was exclaimed by Suruchi”.
“the fish possessed a very big dorsal fin” → “a very big dorsal fin was possessed by the fish”.

Final sentence
It was exclaimed by Suruchi that a very big dorsal fin was possessed by the fish.

Option 2 changes the tense of the that-clause, option 3 changes it to the present, and option 4 is ungrammatical.

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.
The usher must have made the guests sit by the time the dinner was ready. [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: The guests must have been made sit by the usher by the time the dinner was ready.

2.en: The guests must have been made to sit by the usher by the time the dinner was ready.

3.en: The guests must have been made to sit by the usher by the time the dinner had been ready.

4.en: The guests must have made to sit by the usher by the time the dinner had been ready.

solution.en:
Rule
Active make + person + base verb becomes person + be made + to-infinitive in the passive; “must have made” becomes “must have been made”.

Explicit changes
“the guests” becomes the subject.
“must have made … sit” becomes “must have been made to sit”.
Add the agent “by the usher”; the time clause “by the time the dinner was ready” stays unchanged.

Final sentence
The guests must have been made to sit by the usher by the time the dinner was ready.

Option 1 omits “to”, and options 3 and 4 wrongly change the time clause (option 4 also omits “been”).

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

3.en: The restaurant reserved a table for the family by them.

4.en: They were reserving a table for the family at the restaurant.

solution.en:
Rule
If the passive sentence names no agent, supply a general subject such as “they” and keep the tense.

Explicit changes
Add the subject “They”.
“was reserved” becomes “reserved”.
“a table” becomes the object; “for the family at the restaurant” stays.

Final sentence
They reserved a table for the family at the restaurant.

Option 2 changes who reserved the table, option 3 is confused, and option 4 changes the tense.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

3.en: The children decorate the cake for the party.

4.en: The cake decorated the children for the party.

solution.en:
Rule
Simple past passive (was + V3) becomes simple past active (V2).

Explicit changes
The agent “the children” becomes the subject.
“was decorated” becomes “decorated”.
“the cake” becomes the object; “for the party” stays.

Final sentence
The children decorated the cake for the party.

Options 2 and 3 change the tense, and option 4 reverses the roles.

question.en:
Change the following sentence into the Active form.
The construction of the skyscraper is scheduled to have been completed by the end of the year. [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

2.en: They are scheduling to have completed the construction of the skyscraper by the end of the year.

4.en: They are scheduled to have completed the construction of the skyscraper by the end of the year.

solution.en:
Rule
In “is scheduled to have been completed”, the infinitive is passive. Make it active with a general subject (“they”), keeping “are scheduled”.

Explicit changes
Supply the subject “They”.
“is scheduled” becomes “are scheduled” (plural subject).
The passive perfect infinitive becomes active: “to have completed”.
“The construction of the skyscraper” becomes the object.

Final sentence
They are scheduled to have completed the construction of the skyscraper by the end of the year.

Option 1 makes the skyscraper the doer, option 2 uses “are scheduling” with a wrong infinitive, and option 3 is still passive.

question.en:
Change the following sentence into the Active form.
The new theory is said to have been developed over decades. [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: They say that the new theory has been developed over decades.

2.en: They say that the new theory was developed over decades.

3.en: Someone is said to have developed the new theory over decades.

4.en: The new theory developed over decades.

solution.en:
Rule
“Is said to have been + V3” is a passive reporting structure. In the active, use “Someone is said to have + V3”, keeping the perfect infinitive.

Explicit changes
The unknown doer becomes “someone”.
“to have been developed” becomes “to have developed”.
“The new theory” becomes the object.

Final sentence
Someone is said to have developed the new theory over decades.

Options 1 and 2 are still passive, and option 4 changes the meaning.

question.en:
Change the following sentence into the Active form.

2.en: They will have announced the decision before the meeting concludes.

3.en: The decision will be announced before the meeting concludes.

4.en: The meeting will have announced the decision.

solution.en:
Rule
Future perfect passive (will have been + V3) becomes future perfect active (will have + V3); supply “they” for the unnamed agent.

Explicit changes
Add the subject “They”.
“will have been announced” becomes “will have announced”.
“the decision” becomes the object.

Final sentence
They will have announced the decision before the meeting concludes.

Option 1 is ungrammatical, option 3 is passive, and option 4 makes the meeting the doer.

question.en:
Select the correct active form of the given sentence.
"The heavy bag was carefully carried across the room by Jonathan." [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

1.en: Jonathan carefully carrying the heavy bag across the room.

2.en: Jonathan carefully have carried the heavy bag across the room.

3.en: Jonathan carefully carried the heavy bag across the room.

4.en: Jonathan carefully carried the heavy bag the room.

solution.en:
Rule
Passive (simple past): object + was/were + V3 + by + subject
Active (simple past): subject + V2 + object

Explicit changes
by Jonathan → Jonathan becomes the subject
was carried → carried (V2, simple past)
The heavy bag → the heavy bag becomes the object
"carefully" and "across the room" stay unchanged

Final sentence
Jonathan carefully carried the heavy bag across the room.

Option 1 uses the wrong form "carring", option 2 changes the tense to "have carried" with the wrong auxiliary, and option 4 drops "across".

question.en:
Change the following sentence from active to passive:
By the end of the semester, the professors will have been evaluating the thesis papers. [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

solution.en:
Rule
Active (future perfect continuous): will have been + V-ing
Passive: will have been being + V3

Explicit changes
the thesis papers (object) → subject
will have been evaluating → will have been being evaluated
the professors → by the professors
"By the end of the semester" stays unchanged

Final sentence
The thesis papers will have been being evaluated by the professors by the end of the semester.

Options 1 and 3 change the tense to simple past and simple future, and option 2 is not passive at all.

question.en:

Passive: would have been being + V3

Explicit changes
the report drafts (object) → subject
would have been checking → would have been being checked
the supervisor → by the supervisor

Final sentence
The report drafts would have been being checked overnight by the supervisor.

Option 1 changes the tense to past continuous, option 2 is not passive, and option 4 ("would have checked") lacks "been" and is not passive.

question.en:

Passive: may have been being + V3

alternative scenarios (object) → subject

Alternative scenarios may have been being outlined during the session by the deliberation team.

Option 1 is active, and options 2 and 3 drop the modal "may" and change the tense.

question.en:
Change the following active voice sentence into passive voice by selecting the correct option.

Passive: object + is/are + V3 + by + subject

new highways (object) → subject (plural, so "are")
inaugurates → are inaugurated
The Prime Minister → by the Prime Minister
"annually in India" stays unchanged

Final sentence
New highways are inaugurated by the Prime Minister annually in India.

Option 1 changes the tense to past, option 3 is active future, and option 4 changes it to present continuous.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

The agent "his teachers" becomes the subject, and "he" becomes the object "him".

by his teachers → His teachers (subject)
is praised → praise (simple present, plural subject)
he → him (object)

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

Let the work be finished → Finish the work
"by tonight" stays unchanged

question.en:
Change the following active voice sentence into passive voice by selecting the correct option.
They will have completed the railway electrification by next year. [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

Future perfect active (will have + V3) → passive will have been + V3.

Explicit changes
Object "the railway electrification" → subject The railway electrification
will have completed → will have been completed
They → dropped (a general subject is usually omitted)
by next year → unchanged

Final sentence
The railway electrification will have been completed by next year.

Option 1 changes the tense, option 3 uses "completing", and option 4 is not passive (no "been").

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.
People say that the outlaw had helped the destitutes at the time of need. [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

4.en: It is said that the destitutes had been helped at the time of need by the outlaw.

solution.en:
Rule
For "People say that + clause", the passive is It is said that + passive clause. The reporting verb "say" (present) → is said; the past perfect "had helped" → had been helped.

Explicit changes
People say → It is said
Object "the destitutes" → subject the destitutes
had helped → had been helped
the outlaw → by the outlaw

Final sentence
It is said that the destitutes had been helped at the time of need by the outlaw.

Options 1 and 3 change "say" to "was said", and options 2 and 3 use the wrong form "had been being helped".

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

solution.en:
Rule
Present continuous active (is/are + V-ing) → passive is/are + being + V3.

Explicit changes
Object "slogans" → subject Slogans (plural → are)
are shouting → are being shouted
The poor children → by the poor children

Final sentence
Slogans are being shouted by the poor children in the election campaign of the local minister.

Options 2 and 3 change the tense to past ("were"), option 3 also adds a wrong "at", and option 4 uses the present perfect.

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

Explicit changes
Object "a biopic on Amitabh Bachchan covering his college days" → subject (singular → has)
has made → has been made
The producer → by the producer

Final sentence
A biopic on Amitabh Bachchan covering his college days has been made by the producer.

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

Rule
Simple past active (V2) → passive was/were + V3.

Explicit changes
Object "the children flying kites in the park" → subject (plural "children" → were)
photographed → were photographed
The visitors → by the visitors

Final sentence
The children flying kites in the park were photographed by the visitors.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.
The students are made to clean the classroom every day. [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

solution.en:
Rule
With make, the active uses a bare infinitive (make + object + V1), while the passive uses "to" (be made + to + V1). The doer is not stated in the passive, so a suitable subject (the teacher) is supplied in the active.

Explicit changes
are made (simple present passive) → makes (simple present active, singular subject)
Doer supplied → The teacher
The students → object the students
to clean → clean ("to" is dropped after "make" in the active)

Final sentence
The teacher makes the students clean the classroom every day.

Options 2 and 4 lose the sense of being made (forced) to clean, and option 3 is still passive.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

Rule
"needs to be + V3" (passive infinitive) → active "need to + V1". The doer is not stated, so the general subject They is supplied, and "this work" becomes the object.

Explicit changes
Doer supplied → They
needs to be finished → need to finish
This work → object this work

Final sentence
They need to finish this work today.

Option 1 drops "to", option 3 changes the tense to past, and option 4 loses "need to".

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

Rule

Explicit changes
by any of the witnesses → subject None of the witnesses (the negative moves to the subject)
was spoken → spoke
Not a word → object a word
during the trial → unchanged

Final sentence
None of the witnesses spoke a word during the trial.

Option 1 wrongly begins with "Any … did not", option 3 changes the tense to past perfect, and option 4 changes it to present perfect.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

should have been mailed → should have mailed
The letter → object the letter
yesterday → unchanged

John should have mailed the letter yesterday.

Options 2 and 3 change the verb form (and clash with "yesterday"), and option 4 changes the modal "should" to "ought to".

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

The police recovered the stolen painting.

question.en:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.

bought → was bought
He → by him

A new car was bought by him.

question.en:
Select the correct active form of the given sentence.

by the police → subject The police
had been caught → had caught
The notorious thief → object the notorious thief
red-handed, in Hyderabad → unchanged

The police had caught the notorious thief red-handed in Hyderabad.

question.en:
Change the following sentence from active to passive:

the students → by the students
electronically, by the deadline → retained

The assignments must have been being submitted electronically by the students by the deadline.

Such passives are rare in everyday English, but this is the only option that keeps the modal perfect continuous structure. Option 1 lacks "been" before "submitted", option 2 is an active sentence in a different tense, and option 3 drops the modal and changes the tense.

question.en:
Change the following active voice sentence into passive voice by selecting the correct option.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

The house → object the house

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

A psalm on the goddess was written by the pundit when a miraculous incident was seen by him on the occasion of Kumbh Mela.

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.
Somebody has broken the side lamps which had been installed by the municipal corporation last year. [Steno 11 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

solution.en:
Rule
Present perfect active → has/have been + past participle. The subject "somebody" is dropped in the passive.

Explicit changes
has broken the side lamps → the side lamps have been broken
The relative clause "which had been installed by the municipal corporation last year" stays unchanged and stays next to "side lamps".

question.en:

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.
The young artist demanded a good story for the film he was going to act in. [Steno 12 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: A good story for the film he was going to act in was demanded by the young artist.

2.en: A good story for the film he had been going to act in was demanded by the young artist.

3.en: A good story for the film he was going to act in had been demanded by the young artist.

4.en: A good story for the film he had been going to act in had been demanded by the young artist.

solution.en:
Rule: Simple past (demanded) → was/were + V3 (was demanded). The clause “he was going to act in” describes the film and stays unchanged.
Passive: A good story for the film he was going to act in was demanded by the young artist.

Why other options are wrong
Options 2 and 4 needlessly change “was going” to “had been going”; Options 3 and 4 change the main verb to past perfect “had been demanded”.

Therefore, A good story for the film he was going to act in was demanded by the young artist.

question.en:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.
The manager forced the employees to stop using mobiles. [Steno 12 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: The employees to stop using mobiles were forced by the manager.

2.en: The employees were forced to stop by the manager using mobiles.

3.en: The employees were forced by the manager to stop using mobiles.

4.en: The employees by the manager were forced to stop using mobiles.

solution.en:
Rule: Simple past (forced) → were forced. The infinitive phrase “to stop using mobiles” stays attached to the verb it completes.
Passive: The employees were forced by the manager to stop using mobiles.

Why other options are wrong
Option 1 places the infinitive before the verb; Option 2 splits “stop using mobiles”; Option 4 puts “by the manager” before the verb awkwardly.

Therefore, The employees were forced by the manager to stop using mobiles.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.
The meeting is to be held tomorrow. [Steno 12 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

2.en: They have to hold the meeting tomorrow.

3.en: They are to hold the meeting tomorrow.

4.en: They must hold the meeting tomorrow.

solution.en:
Rule: is/are to be + V3 (passive) → is/are to + V1 (active). “is to be held” expresses an arrangement or plan.
Active: They are to hold the meeting tomorrow.

Why other options are wrong
Option 1 loses the sense of arrangement; “have to” and “must” express obligation, not a scheduled plan.

Therefore, They are to hold the meeting tomorrow.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.
The culprit is believed to have fled the country. [Steno 12 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

1.en: People believe the culprit fled the country.

2.en: People are believing the culprit to flee the country.

3.en: It believes the culprit has fled the country.

4.en: People believe the culprit has fled the country.

solution.en:
Rule: “X is believed to have + V3” → People believe (that) X has + V3. The perfect infinitive “to have fled” shows an action completed before the believing, i.e., present perfect “has fled”.
Active: People believe the culprit has fled the country.

Why other options are wrong
Option 1 uses simple past “fled”; Option 2 uses the wrong continuous form “are believing … to flee”; Option 3 uses “It believes”, which has no sensible subject.

Therefore, People believe the culprit has fled the country.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.
It is said that the company will launch a new product next month. [Steno 12 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

2.en: People say that the company launches a new product next month.

3.en: People say the company will launch a new product next month.

4.en: They say the company launched a new product next month.

solution.en:
Rule: “It is said that …” → People say (that) … in the same tense; the reported clause stays unchanged.
Active: People say the company will launch a new product next month.

Why other options are wrong
Option 1 changes “say” to past “said”; Option 2 changes “will launch” to “launches”; Option 4 changes it to “launched”.

Therefore, People say the company will launch a new product next month.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice.
The truth ought to be told to the manager. [Steno 12 Sep 2026 Shift 2]

2.en: Someone must have told the truth to the manager.

3.en: Someone should tell the truth to the manager.

solution.en:
Rule: ought to be + V3 (passive) → ought to + V1 (active). Since no doer is named, use “someone”.
Active: Someone ought to tell the truth to the manager.

Option 2 changes to “must have told”; Option 3 changes “ought to” to “should”; Option 4 makes the manager the one who tells, changing the meaning.

Therefore, Someone ought to tell the truth to the manager.

question.en:

Final sentence
A letter is written by her.

Option 2 uses “was wrote”, option 3 lacks the auxiliary, and option 4 wrongly shifts to past perfect.

question.en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in Direct to Indirect Speech.
She said, "I cannot attend the class today." [Steno 09 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

1.en: She said that she cannot attend the class that day.

2.en: She said that she would not attend the class.

3.en: She said that she could not attend the class that day.

4.en: She said that she might not attend the class.

solution.en:
Rule
With a past reporting verb, the reported clause moves one step back in tense, and pronouns and time words change.

Explicit changes
“I” becomes “she”.
“cannot” becomes “could not”.
“today” becomes “that day”.

Final sentence
She said that she could not attend the class that day.

Option 1 keeps “cannot”; options 2 and 4 change the meaning with “would” and “might” and drop “that day”.

2.en: She said that she was living in Delhi.

3.en: She said that she had lived in Delhi.

4.en: She said that she has lived in Delhi.

solution.en:
Rule
“Used to” (a past habit or state) has no further past form, so it does not change in indirect speech.

Explicit changes
“I” becomes “she”.
“used to live” stays unchanged.

Final sentence
She said that she used to live in Delhi.

“Was living”, “had lived” and “has lived” change the meaning of a past habit.

question.en:

3.en: She said, "I could have left my purse at the café."

4.en: She said, "I must have left my purse at the café."

solution.en:
Rule
While converting indirect speech to direct speech, restore the speaker’s own pronouns and put the words in inverted commas; “might have + past participle” stays unchanged.

Explicit changes
“that she” becomes “I” inside the quotation.
“her purse” becomes “my purse”.
“might have left” is kept as it is.

Final sentence
She said, "I might have left my purse at the café."

“Could” and “must” change the degree of possibility; “may” assumes a back-shift that the reported sentence does not require.

For a wh-question, “said to” becomes “asked”, the wh-word joins the clauses, the word order becomes that of a statement, and the tense moves back.

Explicit changes
“said to” becomes “asked”.
“you” becomes “they”.
“are you making” becomes “they were making” (statement order, past continuous).

Final sentence
The teacher asked the students why they were making so much noise.

Option 2 keeps question order, option 3 is not back-shifted, and “demanded” does not take the listener as an object in this way.

solution.en:

The trainer asked the trainees to go on writing that paragraph till they understood it very clearly.

Keep the reporting verb with its object: “The teacher reminded the students,”.
“to submit their assignments” becomes “Submit your assignments”.

The teacher reminded the students, "Submit your assignments by Friday."

Option 1 turns the instruction into a passive statement, option 2 drops the listeners, and option 4 has the error “should submitted”.

question.en:

solution.en:

“he had been waiting” becomes “I have been waiting”.
“that opportunity” becomes “this opportunity”.

Final sentence
He said, "I have been waiting for this opportunity for years."

Option 1 uses “the” instead of “this”, option 2 wrongly uses “am waiting … for years”, and option 4 changes the tense.

question.en:

solution.en:

“admitted that he had never delivered” becomes said, "I've never delivered".
“that particular topic” becomes “this particular topic”.
“his classes” becomes “my classes”.

The professor said, "I've never delivered a lecture on this particular topic in any of my classes."

question.en:

solution.en:

With “said to” → “told … that”, a reported simple past moves back to the past perfect; a verb already in the past perfect stays unchanged.

Explicit changes
“said to Nirvaan” becomes “told Nirvaan that”.
“He admitted” becomes “he had admitted”.
“he had made” stays “had made”.
“to invest” keeps the base form after “to”.

Pari told Nirvaan that he had admitted that he had made a huge mistake in judgment when he decided to invest all his money in that risky startup company.

Option 2 does not back-shift “admitted”, option 3 changes “had made”, and option 4 has “to invested”.

question.en:

solution.en:

Explicit changes
“Sanvi told Prakash that” becomes Sanvi said to Prakash, "…".

question.en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in Direct Speech.
He said that he had gone to the doctor by the time I called. [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

2.en: He said, "I had gone to the doctor by the time you called."

solution.en:
Rule
To change indirect speech into direct speech, remove "that", put the spoken words in inverted commas and change the pronouns back to the speaker's (he → I, I → you).
The clause "by the time you called" shows that going to the doctor was completed before another past action, so the speaker himself used the past perfect (had + V3), which stays unchanged.

Explicit changes
said that → said, " … ."
he had gone → I had gone (past perfect retained)
by the time I called → by the time you called

Final sentence
He said, "I had gone to the doctor by the time you called."

"By the time + past" needs the past perfect in the main clause, so "have gone", "went" and "go" are all incorrect here.

question.en:

Nothing in the sentence shows a condition, so the Minister's original words were in the simple future.

said that → said, " … ."
would be → will be

Final sentence

question.en:
Convert the following indirect speech sentence into direct speech by selecting the correct option.
The police officer asked whether the suspects had fled the city by then. [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

1.en: The police officer asked, "Did the suspects flee the city by now?"

2.en: The police officer asked, "Had the suspects fled the city by now?"

3.en: The police officer asked, "Have the suspects been fleeing the city by now?"

4.en: The police officer asked, "Have the suspects fled the city by now?"

solution.en:
Rule
While converting an indirect question into a direct question, remove "whether", use question order and add a question mark.
The indirect "by then" goes back to the speaker's "by now". "By now" refers to the present moment, so it needs the present perfect: had fled → have fled.

Explicit changes
asked whether → asked, " … ?"
the suspects had fled → Have the suspects fled
by then → by now

Final sentence
The police officer asked, "Have the suspects fled the city by now?"

"Did … flee by now" (simple past) and "Had … fled by now" (past perfect) do not go with "by now", and "have been fleeing" would become "had been fleeing" in indirect speech.

solution.en:

Explicit changes
said that → said, " … ."
had allocated → has allocated
by then → by now

Final sentence
The Minister said, "The government has allocated additional funds for education by now."

The simple past "allocated" and the past perfect "had allocated" do not go with "by now", and "will allocate" changes the meaning to future.

question.en:
Convert the following direct speech sentence into indirect speech by selecting the correct option.
The Principal said, "Students must submit their projects by Friday." [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 1]

solution.en:
Rule
In indirect speech with a past reporting verb, "must" expressing a present or immediate obligation changes to "had to". "Must" stays unchanged only for permanent truths, rules or prohibitions.
Submitting projects by Friday is a particular obligation, so "must" becomes "had to".

Explicit changes
said, "…" → said that
must submit → had to submit

Final sentence
The Principal said that students had to submit their projects by Friday.

question.en:
Convert the following direct speech sentence into indirect speech by selecting the correct option.

A yes/no question is reported with if/whether, in statement order, without a question mark.
The present perfect changes to the past perfect, and "you" changes to "I" (the listener is the reporter).

asked, "Have you witnessed" → asked if I had witnessed
the question mark → a full stop

The police officer asked if I had witnessed the incident.

question.en:
Convert the following direct speech sentence into indirect speech by selecting the correct option.

said, "Submit" → instructed us to submit
your assignments → our assignments

Final sentence
The Principal instructed us to submit our assignments by Monday.

Options 2, 3 and 4 drop the possessive "our", and "requested" does not suit a principal's instruction.

question.en:

He said to me → He told me that
I will send you → he would send me
when I visit → when he visited

question.en:
Choose the correct indirect narration of the following statement from the given alternatives:

solution.en:
Rule
said to → told; the reported clause is joined by that.
Pronouns change according to the speaker and the listener: you → he (Sailesh), my → her (Sonika).
now → then.
The imaginary condition is shifted back: were → had been and would cry → would have cried.

Explicit changes
said to Sailesh → told Sailesh that
If you were → if he had been
in my place → in her place
now → then
you would cry → he would have cried

Final sentence

Option 2 keeps "now" unchanged, and options 3 and 4 use the wrong pronouns (she/his, she/her).

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Direct Speech.

A universal truth or general statement keeps the present tense in both forms.

said that → said, "
truth is → "Truth is (present tense kept; capital letter inside the quotation)
full stop placed inside the closing inverted comma

The philosopher said, "Truth is often more elusive than fiction."

Options 1 and 3 wrongly change the tense of a general truth, and option 4 changes the meaning to "will always be".

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Direct Speech.

to hold → "Hold (imperative)

question.en:
From the given alternatives, select the correct indirect narration of the given direct narration.

says, "…" → says that

question.en:

question.en:

question.en:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.

Explicit changes
said to the students → warned the students that
If you don't keep quiet → if they didn't keep quiet
I shall send you out → he would send them out

Final sentence
The teacher warned the students that if they didn't keep quiet, he would send them out.

Option 2 uses "don't kept" and "shall", option 3 keeps "shall", and option 4 uses "asked … if", which does not suit a warning.

question.en:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect Speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct Speech.
He said to the scientist, "How long will it take to reach Mars with this propulsion system?" [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 3]

1.en: He asked the scientist how long it will take to reach Mars with this propulsion system.

2.en: He told the scientist how long it would take to reach Mars with that propulsion system.

3.en: He asked the scientist how long it would take to reach Mars with that propulsion system.

4.en: He asked the scientist that how long it would take to reach Mars with that propulsion system.

solution.en:
Rule
A wh-question is reported with asked, the wh-word acts as the connector (no "that"), the question becomes a statement (subject before verb), and the tense is back-shifted.

Explicit changes
said to → asked
"How long will it take" → how long it would take
this → that
question mark → full stop

Final sentence
He asked the scientist how long it would take to reach Mars with that propulsion system.

Option 1 keeps "will" and "this", option 2 uses "told" for a question, and option 4 wrongly adds "that" before the wh-word.

question.en:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Indirect Speech. Choose the correct Direct Speech form.
The meteorologist said that it might rain heavily in the hills. [Steno 10 Sep 2026 Shift 3]

1.en: The meteorologist said, "It might rain heavily in the hills."

2.en: The meteorologist said, "It will rain heavily in the hills."

3.en: The meteorologist said, "It may rain heavily in the hills."

4.en: The meteorologist said, "It rained heavily in the hills."

solution.en:
Rule
While changing indirect speech to direct speech, "said that" becomes said, "…" and the reported words are placed within inverted commas. The modal might does not change in reported speech, so the direct speech that matches the reported sentence keeps might.

Explicit changes
said that → said, "…"
it might rain → "It might rain …"
in the hills → unchanged

Final sentence
The meteorologist said, "It might rain heavily in the hills."

Option 2 turns a possibility into a certainty ("will"), option 4 changes it into a past event ("rained"), and option 3 alters the modal given in the sentence.

question.en:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Indirect Speech. Choose the correct Direct Speech form.

Rule
A general truth or scientific fact keeps its tense and modal in reported speech, so the direct speech also keeps can.

Explicit changes
said that → said, "…"
too much sugar can harm the liver → "Too much sugar can harm the liver."

Final sentence
The doctor said, "Too much sugar can harm the liver."

Options 2, 3 and 4 change the modal ("may", "could") or the verb form ("harms"), which alters the meaning.

question.en:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Indirect Speech. Choose the correct Direct Speech form.

told the players that → said, "…"
they → you
their → your
must → must

Final sentence
The coach said, "You must give your best during the finals."

Options 2 and 3 keep the third-person pronouns inside the quotation, and option 4 changes "must" to "have to".

question.en:
Convert the following direct speech sentence into indirect speech by selecting the correct option.

Option 2 does not back-shift the tense, option 3 changes the meaning to the present continuous, and option 4 uses the simple past.

question.en:

said to → told

inverted commas removed

question.en:
Choose the correct indirect narration of the following statement from the given alternatives:

solution.en:

When the reporting verb is in the past, the simple past changes to the past perfect; first-person pronouns change to match the speaker.

said, "…" → said that
I → she, my → her
did not believe → had not believed
saw → had seen

Final sentence
Niyati said that she had not believed her eyes when she had seen him dance.

Option 1 uses "did not believed" (wrong), option 2 changes only one verb, and option 3 does not back-shift the tenses.

question.en:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Direct Speech.

solution.en:

said that → said, "…"
he → I
had been trying → have been trying
the previous morning → yesterday morning

Final sentence
He said, "I have been trying to book the tickets since yesterday morning."

Option 2 keeps the past perfect continuous, and options 3 and 4 change the tense and keep "the previous morning".

question.en:

Rimjhim asked Barsha if she was making a portrait of the beggar sitting in front of her.

question.en:

question.en:

question.en:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Indirect Speech. Choose the correct Direct Speech form.

question.en:

question.en:

question.en:

question.en:

question.en:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech:

solution.en:
Rule
Third conditional sentences (past unreal counterfactual: Had + Subject + V3, Subject + would have + V3) do not shift back further in tense when converted between direct and indirect speech because the past perfect is already the most remote past.

Explicit changes
• Remove the subordinating conjunction 'that'.
• Enclose the conditional clause directly inside quotation marks.
• Retain the inverted conditional structure: 'Had the data been normalized, the projections would have aligned better.'

Final sentence
"Had the data been normalized, the projections would have aligned better," commented the analyst.

Options 2, 3, and 4 distort the meaning entirely.
